fable-5.1.text:
I'll be honest that I only saw it from one seat, so take this as one person's view rather than some verdict on the company.

The biggest change I noticed was just scale. When I arrived, it still felt like a research lab that happened to have a product. You could walk over and argue with someone about a paper, and that argument could actually change what the team worked on next week. By the time I was thinking about leaving, it felt more like a company that had research inside it. That's not a criticism. It's what success does. More people, more customers, more revenue, more things that can break. The coordination cost goes up, and the room for a single researcher to just follow a hunch goes down a bit.

The second thing was the center of gravity shifting toward the agent and coding side. Early on, a lot of the energy was around alignment, interpretability, "what is this model actually doing." Those teams were still there and still serious, but the thing everyone was watching day to day became usage, how well the model performs for people building on it, how it does on long tasks. For me that was actually interesting, because that's the direction I'd been pushing on since ReAct and SWE-bench. But it does change the texture of conversations. You talk more about evals and deployment, less about open-ended questions.

And then the third thing, which is more subtle, is that the culture became more careful about what gets said externally. Not in a bad way, I think it's responsible. But as a researcher who likes to write and share half-baked ideas, you feel that. Some of what I wanted to think about out loud was easier to do from outside.

What stayed the same was the people. I genuinely think it's one of the highest-density places for thoughtful people I've been. The reason I left wasn't that the culture went bad. It was more that I wanted to work on a different set of problems, with a different kind of freedom, and that's hard to get inside any lab at that size. So I'd say the culture changed in the way a growing organization has to, and I changed too, and at some point those two paths just stopped overlapping as much.

r001.rationale: The response describes organizational growth and shifting priorities, but it does not suggest that clashes between newcomers and Anthropic’s original culture caused cultural disorder.

Those are different questions, and I wouldn’t want to collapse them into one sweeping judgment.
